articles.title: The Binance hack exploited familiar weaknesses – all organisations should learn from it
articles.author: Bogdan Księżopolski, Head of the Institute of Computer Science, Head of Cybersecurity Department, Kozminski University
paras: Hackers have stolen around US$6.3 billion (£4.7 billion) from the cryptocurrency exchange Binance, most of which was taken in under an hour. According to Binance, the attack exploited systems and individuals with the authority to carry out transactions involving such large sums.

Such vulnerabilities exist everywhere; statistics show that people and the systems they directly use, including their personal computers, remain a top target for cybercriminals. All organisations could therefore learn lessons from this attack.

The Binance theft took place on the evening of October 29, 2026. The Binance attack netted four times the amount stolen in the previous biggest cryptocurrency theft, on the Bybit exchange in February 2025.

Private keys, used to authorise spending or withdrawal from crypto-wallets, are a known vulnerability. But Binance found no evidence these were leaked. An initial statement from the exchange pointed to a compromised laptop belonging to an engineer. This gave the attacker access to the internal system that processes withdrawal requests.

Because blockchain transactions can be fully audited, investigators can trace the events leading up to the attack. On October 28, the address from which the theft was later carried out received 0.3 ETH (Ether cryptocurrency) from Tornado Cash, a service that mixes funds from multiple users to hide their origin.

A few hours before the theft, a malicious smart contract (computer code that automatically runs when certain conditions are met) was deployed from the same address. At 20:20:59 UTC, a transaction was sent from that address containing 50 signed authorisations intended to transfer control of a Binance wallet to that smart contract. One of them was accepted by a Binance hot wallet (a wallet used by the exchange to process customer withdrawals).

Following this takeover, the hackers proceeded to empty the hot wallet of 64 different tokens worth approximately $2.5 billion (£1.8 billion) in a single transaction. Other wallets were then emptied in parallel using standard signed transactions, bringing the total amount stolen to $6.3 billion. Valid Binance digital signatures were needed for draining the wallets, but how the attackers obtained these has not been explained.
The same audit trail shows that the attackers were rehearsing several hours earlier, but at that stage, nothing linked them to Binance.

The 2025 attack on Bybit, which resulted in the theft of US$1.5 billion (£1.1 billion), also appears to have involved a compromised laptop that was capable of performing operations requiring high-level privileges.

North Korean cybercriminals, who were implicated in the attack on the Bybit exchange by analysts, specialise in creating so-called “legends”. These are identities created to deceive companies and individuals. In October, the US Department of Justice indicted 14 individuals in a case in which North Korean cybercriminals, using stolen or fabricated identities, secured remote jobs at more than 70 US companies.

Two days before the attack, Binance reported that, for a week, it had been blocking North Korea-linked attack attempts involving fake recruiters. Was this related to the attack? We don’t know yet, but the modus operandi is well recognised and widespread. North Korea, meanwhile, has denied allegations that it was behind the attack.

A cybercriminal can use a legend to pose for months as a hardworking employee, a cheap and reliable contractor, or as a generous employer. The criminal waits for the moment when a crucial software installation is carried out or a vital document is signed. Since a large amount of today’s work involves only digital interactions with people, it is sensible to approach every new contact with limited trust.

A good example of how such legends work is the attack on the Japanese DMM Bitcoin exchange in 2024, which netted US$308 million (£230 million) for the attackers. The hacker posed as a recruiter on LinkedIn and gained the trust of a Ginco employee.

Ginco is a company that provides DMM with wallet management software. The recruiter offered the Ginco employee a job on the condition that they completed a recruitment test. The test URL actually led to a malicious Python script; from this point on, the victim’s computer was compromised.
This is classic social engineering. In this case, the target was a cryptocurrency wallet system accessed through a compromised computer. About two months later, the attackers drained funds from DMM.

Virtually all businesses should learn from such attacks. The first lesson concerns what their computer systems are allowed to authorise. Traditionally, cryptographic keys are protected using devices known as hardware security modules and multi-signature schemes (where multiple private keys are required to authorise an action).

Unfortunately, such mechanisms do not protect against an attack launched from a compromised internal system controlled by a hacker. It is advisable to define rules for authorising financial transactions, set time and amount limits, and require approval via an alternative channel for unusual requests.

Additionally, since most of the funds in the Binance cyberattack were transferred within an hour, computer systems should have mechanisms in place to block suspicious transactions within seconds, without waiting for approval from the on-duty security engineer.

The second lesson is about recruitment, which has evolved into a security mechanism. North Korean cybercriminals use stolen or fabricated identities and virtual private networks (VPNs) to pose as people living in the US.

Visual identities during online interviews can be falsified using deepfakes. Video interviews and CVs no longer prove who someone really is. In some cases, actors are even hired for in-person interviews. Today, we need to focus on strengthening the identity verification process. It’s important to check candidates through independently verified contacts during this process.

The third lesson concerns the work computers of individuals with privileged access to the computer system. Typically, organisations have protected themselves against phishing through training and email filters.
Unfortunately, some of the attacks described above bypass the filters that are currently in use because they target specific victims (an act known as spear phishing).

In the case of Bybit, gaining access to a developer’s computer allowed the attacker to seize session tokens in the cloud and bypass multi-factor authentication. One possible solution is to separate privileged access from day-to-day operations.

To this end, access to withdrawal systems should only be permitted from company-managed dedicated devices, and computer code received from external sources should only be executed in an isolated environment.

The largest cryptocurrency theft in history is essentially a story about how people and processes are the weakest links in security systems. Cryptography was not compromised and remains a key security measure. Unfortunately, these same vulnerabilities exist in banks, payment companies and hospitals and attackers are well aware of them.

articles.title: NASA’s Swift telescope has burned up, months after a robot sent to save it failed – here’s why it’s so hard to boost a satellite
articles.author: Wanjiku Chebet Kanjumba, Ph.D. Candidate in Aerospace Engineering, University of Florida
paras: NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory took its last look at the sky on Oct. 20, 2026, while orbiting about 171 miles (275 kilometers) above Earth. NASA ended the telescope’s mission three days later, because Swift had sunk so low that drag from the thin air there meant its telescopes couldn’t hold steady. The telescope reentered the atmosphere on Nov. 4 above the North Sumatra region of Indonesia and largely burned up, an abrupt ending to two decades spent observing powerful cosmic explosions.

Swift’s reentry comes after a failed rescue mission in the summer of 2026. LINK, a commercial robotic spacecraft sent to raise Swift into a safer orbit, reentered Earth’s atmosphere in September. The machine designed to save a falling satellite burned up first.
As a Ph.D. candidate in aerospace engineering, I know that rescuing satellites is hard. I research how spacecraft approach and capture satellites, including objects that tumble uncontrollably.

Swift’s loss points to a new hazard for the young industry that repairs, refuels and moves spacecraft around in orbit. If something goes wrong, the spacecraft doing the rescuing can become another problem.
The rescuer started spinning

The plan was for LINK to approach Swift, grab it with one of its three robotic arms and fire its thrusters to push the telescope back up to about 373 miles (600 kilometers) above Earth’s surface, where it could keep observing for years.

In late July, LINK lost two of its three reaction wheels, which are heavy wheels inside a spacecraft that help it turn without using fuel. That loss, combined with problems with its propulsion system, sent the spacecraft into an uncontrolled spin.
Without working wheels, a spacecraft steers with its thrusters instead, and every burn spends propellant.

Engineers eventually slowed LINK’s rotation by firing its thrusters against the spin. NASA reported in August that they had cut its spin from about nine degrees per second to roughly one and a half degrees per second.

NASA and Katalyst Space, LINK’s builder, called off the capture and boost later in August. The team still flew LINK within 7.5 to 9 miles (12 to 15 kilometers) of Swift, where it deployed LINK’s three robotic arms and tested its electric thrusters. It never got close enough to grab the telescope.

A servicing spacecraft, like LINK, launches with a finite supply of propellant. Engineers split that fuel supply among the mission’s jobs, from reaching the target and approaching it safely to capturing it and moving it to a new orbit. They also pack some extra fuel in case of surprises.
Think of a tow truck that burns most of its gas getting itself out of a ditch. Even if it reaches a broken-down car, it may not have enough fuel left to tow it home.

That scenario is close to what happened to LINK. Even after engineers brought its spin under control, Katalyst said the spacecraft no longer had enough propellant to capture Swift and raise its orbit safely.

A fuel budget that covers only the planned steps leaves nothing for recovering from a fault. But every extra pound of propellant also makes a spacecraft heavier, and heavier spacecraft cost more to launch and take more fuel to move.
Speed buys time and costs backup

Starting in 2024, solar activity swelled Earth’s upper atmosphere, and the extra drag pulled Swift down faster than expected. Once NASA saw how quickly Swift was falling, the agency had to move fast to try to save the observatory. Space missions typically take years to develop and launch, but in this case, a slow, conventional development program risked arriving too late.
NASA awarded Katalyst a US$30 million contract in September 2025. The company had less than a year to design, build, test and launch LINK. LINK launched on July 3, 2026.

Speed comes with trade-offs. In engineering, a compressed schedule can leave less time for repeated testing, building spare hardware and planning recovery options. Public reports do not say whether that trade-off played any part in LINK’s faults.

NASA has said that even though LINK didn’t succeed, the effort gave the agency experience in quickly building, launching and operating a servicing spacecraft. Engineers also showed they could upload new control software to steady a damaged servicing spacecraft with the hardware it had left. And LINK tested its arms and fired all three thrusters at once in orbit.

While Swift was the most pressing case for a boost mission, it’s not the only one. NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope could one day use a similar boost, and news reports suggested it would have been next in line had this mission worked.

Future missions are pursuing two complementary approaches for rescuing satellites. Astroscale’s ELSA-M is built to capture satellites that carry a docking plate installed before launch, which would make it easier for a rescuer to snag and boost them if the satellite eventually got into trouble. The European Space Agency’s ClearSpace-1 is planned for 2029 and aims to capture the Proba-1 satellite, which doesn’t have a docking plate or anything to help ClearSpace-1 capture it, and remove it from orbit.

LINK’s mission showed that a rescue takes more than a robotic arm and enough thrust to reach a target. It also takes a servicer spacecraft that can stay stable, recover from its own faults and keep enough propellant reserved to finish the job. In Swift’s case, the rescuer fell short before the rescue could begin.

articles.title: NASA’s Swift Observatory has burned up in the atmosphere – the indispensable telescope helped astronomers track fast-moving events in space
articles.author: Mary Ogborn, Ph.D. Candidate in Astrophysics, Penn State
paras: A 22-year-old space telescope lost its fight against gravity and came crashing down to Earth on the morning of Nov. 4, 2026, above the North Sumatra region of Indonesia. The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory had been the go-to telescope for observing astrophysical events that happen quickly, such as supernovas. Its onboard instruments allowed it to contribute greatly to many subfields of science.
Swift was not classified as a flagship observatory, like the Hubble Space Telescope or Chandra X-Ray Observatory, but it left behind a legacy that will not swiftly be forgotten.

The Swift Observatory first came onto the scene in 2004 when NASA launched it into low Earth orbit. Originally called the Swift Gamma-Ray Burst Explorer, its purpose was to move quickly to follow up on explosive events called gamma-ray bursts and their afterglows using its three onboard telescopes.

Swift’s name is not an acronym. Instead, it refers to its speed and likens the observatory to the bird. It could rotate and move quickly to observe transient events, which are events that happen quickly and fade away.
Watching for gamma-ray bursts

Gamma-ray bursts are the most explosive and energetic events in the universe. Scientists theorize they come from the explosions of large stars or mergers of a very dense type of star called neutron stars. Gamma-ray bursts, as the name implies, release large bursts of gamma-rays, but as these explosions fade, they lose energy. Scientists can spot remnants of gamma-ray bursts by looking for X-rays and optical light as the gamma rays themselves fade.

Swift’s burst alert telescope could see light in the gamma-ray portion of the electromagnetic spectrum, so it searched directly for gamma-ray bursts. Its X-ray telescope and ultraviolet-optical telescope could measure the resulting afterglow of X-ray and UV light these events produced as they faded.

What set Swift apart was its ability to do what’s called slewing: In order to follow up on transient events, it swiveled its telescopes around quickly and could cover 50 degrees in less than 75 seconds. Comparatively, it takes Hubble about 15 minutes to turn 90 degrees.
By 2015, just 10 years after science operations started, Swift detected its 1,000th gamma-ray burst.

Swift’s ability to slew quickly allowed it to detect more than just gamma-ray bursts. Its onboard instruments could detect anything that changes quickly in the sky, including supernovae and X-ray flares from binary stars, which are two stars bound by gravity that tend to interact with each other. It could also detect the electromagnetic counterparts to gravitational waves, which result from large distortions in space-time, such as the merger of dense objects such as black holes and neutron stars.

In 2008, when observing another supernova, Swift by chance detected a slight rise in X-rays, which preceded a supernova explosion. This initial increase in X-rays represented the earliest phase of supernova evolution ever observed. Swift’s extensive alert network notified astronomers all over the world who were able to point other space- and ground-based telescopes at the supernova to follow up and obtain even more data.

Then in 2017, when the IceCube Neutrino Observatory – whose principal investigator Francis Halzen won the 2026 Nobel Prize in physics – detected high-energy neutrinos, Swift was able to help localize their source. Neutrinos are massless particles that do not interact with most matter. This property makes it hard for physicists to detect them and pinpoint their source. Scientists know that astrophysical events can emit them, and they used Swift to connect these neutrinos to a very energetic supermassive black hole at the center of its galaxy.

In 2025, Swift detected a compound called hydroxyl on the interstellar object 3I/ATLAS, indicating the presence of water. This result may help answer the question of how Earth obtained water on its surface. Some theories propose that comets and interstellar objects bombarded the Earth in the early solar system and deposited water.

Swift’s journey took a turn in 2024 and 2025, as the Sun became more active. These years were in a period known as a solar maximum, when more solar flares, or explosions on the surface of the Sun, released matter and high-energy particles that hit Earth’s atmosphere.

Because of this increase in space weather, many people as far south as Pennsylvania were able to see the northern lights. While this activity produced jaw-dropping views, it also exerted pressure on satellites. Solar particles can exert a small force on whatever they hit, and when there are many, that force multiplies.

This force pushed against Swift, which lived in low Earth orbit at about 373 miles (600 kilometers) above Earth’s surface. The telescope eventually reentered the atmosphere, where drag pulled it down toward Earth.
NASA partnered with a company called Katalyst Space Technologies and launched a mission to boost Swift back into its orbit on July 3, 2026.

Unfortunately, this mission failed, and Swift reentered and burned up in Earth’s atmosphere in early November. The observatory didn’t hit the surface fully intact. Instead, it mostly burned up on its way in.

The loss of such an observatory is a tough blow to the astronomical community, which was gearing up to use the satellite in conjunction with the new Vera C. Rubin Observatory. However, astronomers will continue to remember Swift’s team and their countless accomplishments and discoveries.
Editor’s note: This article was updated on Nov. 4, 2026, to reflect when and where Swift reentered the atmosphere.

articles.title: How space weather powers auroras in the sky and threatens power grids on the ground
articles.author: Sanjay Kumar, Research Fellow in Climate and Space Sciences and Engineering, University of Michigan
paras: An aurora is one of nature’s most spectacular light shows: It looks like green or red curtains rippling across the night sky. When viewed from the ground, this colorful display might seem far away and disconnected from anything happening on Earth’s surface.

But while these beautiful displays are part of a much larger process known as “space weather” – changes in Earth’s space environment caused by activity from the Sun – they’re closely connected to electric currents that can flow through the ground under your feet.

Space weather can create a spectacle in the sky, while also driving electric currents that can damage power grids and other technological systems on the ground. Space physicists like us want to understand how space weather can affect infrastructure on Earth.

Our research shows that a single space weather event called a substorm, during which energy is released tens of thousands of miles away from Earth, can affect the ground within minutes. The strength of the impact can vary from place to place depending on the latitude and the structure of the soil and rock below your feet.
From solar storm to substorm
Earth is constantly immersed in the solar wind: a stream of charged particles flowing outward from the Sun. Occasionally, the Sun releases a much larger eruption called a coronal mass ejection.

This cloud of charged particles and magnetic fields does not simply “hit” Earth and immediately cause power-grid failures. Instead, it can set off a chain of processes in space that can pose a threat to power grids.

First, when the coronal mass ejection reaches Earth, the charged particles and magnetic fields it carries interact with Earth’s magnetosphere. The magnetosphere is the region of space around Earth dominated by its magnetic field.

If the coronal mass ejection’s magnetic field is oriented in a certain way, it can connect with Earth’s magnetic field on the side facing the Sun. The solar wind then carries these connected field lines around Earth away from the Sun and stretches them far out into space behind Earth. This process forms a long region of stretched magnetic field lines called the magnetotail.

Magnetic energy builds up in the magnetotail as the solar wind continues to push the field lines farther into space – until they come close enough to reconnect. Then, the stored energy is released in an explosive process known as a substorm. This release occurs on the side of Earth facing away from the Sun, roughly 28,000 to 40,000 miles (45,000 to 65,000 kilometers) from Earth.

During the substorm, energetic particles shoot along the magnetic field lines toward Earth. When these particles collide with oxygen and nitrogen atoms in the upper atmosphere, about 56 to 93 miles (90 to 150 kilometers) overhead, they produce the glowing aurora.
These energetic particles also drive strong electrical currents in Earth’s upper atmosphere. Rapid changes in these currents can cause Earth’s magnetic field at the ground level to change sharply.
These changing magnetic fields can induce electric currents in the ground and in power lines, potentially damaging transformers and tripping circuit breakers.
From the magnetotail to Earth’s surface
Our team wanted to find out how closely the aurora is linked to disturbances in Earth’s magnetic field and how long it takes for a disturbance released in the magnetotail to reach Earth’s surface.

We examined two auroral events in detail by combining data from NASA spacecraft – including THEMIS, time history of events and macroscale interactions during substorms, and NOAA’s GOES, geostationary operational environmental satellites – with data from a dense network of magnetometers across Arctic Canada that measure changes in Earth’s magnetic field at the ground. These changes in the magnetic field can drive electric currents in the ground and power lines.

The observations revealed a clear sequence. When these stretched magnetic field lines on the nightside suddenly reconnected, the spacecraft recorded an abrupt change in the magnetic field and a burst of charged particles moving toward Earth. About seven minutes later, the magnetic field at the ground began to change rapidly. The effects of this energy release, tens of thousands of miles away, reached Earth’s surface within minutes.
The aurora and ground disturbance do not appear everywhere at once. In our observations, they began at lower latitudes and then spread toward the North Pole over the next 20 to 30 minutes.

Nearby geomagnetic stations, however, often recorded very different responses. Stations tens to hundreds of miles apart could see strong magnetic swings at one site and weak ones at another. The difference depended on the strength of currents in Earth’s upper atmosphere and local conditions – including how electrically conductive the upper atmosphere is overhead and how conductive the ground beneath the magnetic station is. This atmospheric conductivity can vary with sunlight and auroral activity, while ground conductivity depends on local geology and moisture levels.
Seeing a spectacular aurora does not automatically mean the ground beneath it is experiencing the strongest magnetic disturbances or electric currents.
When the aurora becomes a grid problem

History shows that space weather poses a real risk to space and ground infrastructure. During a March 1989 geomagnetic storm, people witnessed spectacular auroras as far south as Texas, while rapid changes in magnetic fields contributed to the collapse of the Hydro-Québec power system. More than 6 million people lost electricity for about nine hours on a cold winter night. With the city lights extinguished, the aurora appeared even more spectacular.

A similar combination occurred during the Halloween storms of October 2003. Auroras illuminated skies across Europe, while geomagnetically induced currents contributed to a blackout affecting about 50,000 people in Malmö, Sweden.

Recently, during the May 2024 geomagnetic storm – the strongest in over two decades – geomagnetically induced currents stressed the power grid in southern Sweden, forcing a transmission link to disconnect and temporarily interrupting the flow of electricity through that part of the grid.

Space weather forecasts can warn power grid operators hours before solar activity reaches Earth, giving them time to monitor grid conditions and prepare for possible disruptions. But the effects of substorms, including potential risks to power grids, develop after the solar wind interacts with Earth’s magnetic environment. Our research shows that these effects unfold on timescales of minutes.

The next time the aurora ripples across the night sky, remember that the colorful light shining overhead is only one part of a larger process. Tens of thousands of miles away, an explosive release of magnetic energy may have just taken place. Within minutes, its effects can begin to reach the ground.
The beauty of the aurora and the risk of power-grid disruption from invisible currents above and below are two faces of the same space weather event.

articles.title: We used ancient DNA to track the origins and spread of the Germanic and Celtic languages – new research
articles.author: Guus Kroonen, Associate Professor,  Scandinavian, Germanic and Indo-European Comparative Linguistics, Leiden University; University of Copenhagen
paras: Why do people speak Germanic languages such as English in England and Swedish in Sweden, but Celtic languages in Ireland, Wales and Brittany? The dispersal of languages is one of the enigmas of European prehistory.
Two new studies in Nature, which we took part in, show how DNA from several thousand ancient individuals helps us solve this riddle.

As early as the 17th century, scholars noticed striking similarities between the European languages. English father, Swedish fader, Irish athair, Latin pater and Greek patḗr do not resemble each other by coincidence. Today, we know that these languages, together with Baltic, Slavic, Indic and Iranian, evolved from a common ancestor: Proto-Indo-European.

But how did this ancestral language come to be spoken so widely across Eurasia? During the 19th and 20th centuries, a wide variety of theories were developed about its origin. One of these placed its homeland on the vast grassy steppes north of the Black and Caspian Seas around 5,000 years ago.
Subsequent migrations by the pastoral nomads of the Yamnaya culture are thought to have spread the ancestral language across Europe and Asia.

The occurrence of such a migration, inferred from archaeology, was debated for over a century with the answer seemingly lost to time. However, thanks to ancient DNA, we now know that large groups of people migrated from the Eastern European steppes to Europe around 5,000 years ago, providing compelling support for the spread of Indo-European languages from that region.

Today, the spread of Indo-European languages from the steppes is accepted by most historical linguists. Yet several questions remain: how did the individual Indo-European languages subsequently spread to their historically known locations?

As part of an international collaboration, led by researchers from the University of Copenhagen in Denmark and Leiden University in the Netherlands, we analysed the DNA of thousands of prehistoric Europeans, including more than 700 newly sequenced individuals. This allowed us to test, for the first time, specific theories on the prehistoric dispersals of the Germanic and Celtic languages.
The first Germanic speakers in Northern Europe?

It has long been assumed that the earliest form of Germanic arrived in Scandinavia with the first steppe migrants around 4,800 years ago. This event would then have been followed by several millennia of linguistic and genetic continuity.
Our analyses yielded a surprisingly different result. Around 4,000 years ago, a second group with steppe ancestry appeared in Eastern Scandinavia, probably arriving from across the Baltic Sea.

This previously unknown population spread across much of Scandinavia, ultimately matching the region where the ancestral form of Germanic is believed to have been spoken during the first millennium BC.

This distribution, combined with their ancestry persisting in most later Germanic-speaking populations, suggests these newcomers may have introduced the precursor of the Germanic languages, some 800 years later than traditionally assumed. In this scenario, the timeline for the language history of Northern Europe is reset.
Anglo-Saxons and Vikings share a surprising past

Our understanding of the regions where specific Germanic languages were spoken suddenly comes into focus around 2,000 years ago. At this point, writing spread to northern Europe in the form of the runic alphabet, allowing us to compare migrations with the spread of the Germanic languages we still know today.

By around 2,000 years ago, people from Scandinavia began spreading south, into present-day Poland, Germany and the Netherlands. During the Migration Period, beginning around 400 AD, related populations from around northern Germany subsequently dispersed across Europe. Among them were the West Germanic-speaking Anglo-Saxons, who settled in England and the Langobards, who ultimately established a kingdom in Italy.

But we also discovered a migration in the opposite direction. People from northern Germany and southern Jutland, still largely descending from Eastern Scandinavians, moved back into Denmark and southern Sweden. Intriguingly, they were closely related to the ancestors of the Anglo-Saxons who migrated to England, which may help explain similar art styles and cultural elements between the regions.

This migration coincided with major cultural changes in Southern Scandinavia, the emergence of new political centers and the earliest stages in the development of Old Norse, the language of the Vikings.
Norway, however, tells a different story. Despite remaining largely unaffected by this migration, pre-Viking Age Norwegians still participated in the linguistic changes that gave rise to Old Norse.
This suggests that linguistic changes spread not only through migration, but also through cultural contact between closely related Scandinavian communities.
A new perspective on the origins of Celtic

Before the spread of Germanic and the expansion of the Roman Empire, Celtic languages were spoken across much of Europe, from Spain and France to southern Germany and the Balkans. Today, they survive mainly along the Atlantic coast, particularly in Ireland, Wales and Brittany.

The origins of the Celtic languages have also long been debated. Some scholars propose that they emerged along the Atlantic and subsequently spread eastwards. Others place their origins in Central Europe, in the context of the Bronze Age Urnfield and successive Iron Age Hallstatt and La Tène cultures.

Our genetic analyses provide the strongest support for the latter scenario. Between 3,200 and 2,800 years ago, ancestry associated with populations of the Urnfield culture expanded westward into France and Great Britain, eventually reaching northeastern Spain. This closely matches the model for the spread of Celtic from central Europe.

However, an earlier Atlantic migration from southwestern Europe into Britain, around 3,800 years ago, offers partial support for theories proposing western Celtic origins, indicating the process was potentially more complex.

Ancient DNA cannot reveal the language or languages a particular individual spoke. But by comparing prehistoric population movements with archaeological and linguistic evidence, we can increasingly test competing theories about how languages spread.

Our studies reveal a complex European past in which populations, cultures and languages develop through repeated migrations, contact and mixture. Thanks to ancient DNA, we can now reconstruct that history with unprecedented precision.

articles.title: Seeing is no longer believing: why physical witnesses matter more in the age of AI-generated content
articles.author: Oliver Bray, Dean of Leeds School of Arts, Leeds Beckett University
paras: When Elon Musk unveiled Tesla’s latest Roadster, much of the attention focused on the obvious spectacle. Here, apparently, was one of the oldest promises of science fiction finally made real: a flying car.

The demonstration had everything you might expect from contemporary technological theatre. Watching the futuristic vehicle on a looping track climb, flip and descend, it was difficult not to think of Hot Wheels tracks, science-fiction films and the illustrations of the future that filled children’s books during the latter half of the 20th century.

Yet what struck me most, as a researcher in performance and public communication, was not the car itself but the audience. The event was livestreamed, captured from multiple camera angles and quickly circulated online. People were also assembled to witness it physically. Most revealingly, Musk reportedly remarked that the live audience was there so nobody would think the footage had been made with AI. In a single sentence, he captured one of the defining cultural anxieties of the present moment: seeing is increasingly not enough when it comes to believing.

For more than a century, technologies of reproduction progressively reduced the importance of physical presence. In The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction, the cultural critic Walter Benjamin connected authenticity to an original’s particular “presence in time and space”. Photography allowed us to see somewhere we had not been, film extended that principle, television took it further and the internet collapsed geography altogether. For a time, the photograph or moving image acquired its own evidential authority: seeing something recorded was, with reasonable caveats, grounds for accepting that an event had occurred.

Artificial intelligence unsettles that relationship. Convincing images can now depict events that never happened. Deepfakes can simulate people saying things they never said. The significant change is that increasingly persuasive representations of reality need not have an originating event in the physical world.

This creates a curious reversal. The more sophisticated our technologies of representation become, the less the image alone can tell us about where it came from. In that context, the crowd at the Tesla demonstration acquires an unexpected function: they didn’t merely witness the evidence, they became a part of it. Audience members produced their own recordings and images, so credibility no longer rested entirely with Tesla’s official footage. The event acquired a form of distributed corroboration.

But there is an important problem here. Human witnesses are not reliable simply because they are human. When magician David Copperfield made the Statue of Liberty appear to disappear on television in April 1983, a live audience formed an essential part of the illusion. Around 50 million television viewers reportedly watched, but those physically present could truthfully say they had seen the statue apparently vanish – although it had, of course, gone nowhere. Copperfield’s audience didn’t authenticate an explanation of reality, it authenticated an experience.

So an event can be real, but witnesses do not always convert spectacle into truth. Audiences can be manipulated or incorporated into the performance they appear to authenticate. A hundred recordings of an illusion remain recordings of an illusion.
Perhaps the question then becomes not simply whether an image is real, but one about provenance. Where did that image come from and who is prepared to account for it?

Synthetic media (text, image, audio, video, or 3D assets that are artificially created, modified, or generated) doesn’t need a camera with an object in front of it, or even for a depicted scene to exist. This changes the nature of authenticity.

I have explored a related problem through the idea of the “unapproved orator”. Public communication increasingly reaches us through layers of speechwriting, editing, platforms, algorithms and summaries. The difficulty is not simply determining whether statements are true or false, but establishing whose voice we are really encountering and who ultimately stands behind it. Synthetic media pushes this further by allowing representations to circulate while their human origin, and therefore accountability, becomes increasingly difficult to establish.

A witness cannot resolve that problem. People can be wrong, lie or misunderstand what they have experienced. But a witness is present and can potentially be questioned. A witness can locate themselves within the event and say: “I was there”. In a sense, we borrow their presence. Perhaps that is what becomes valuable when images cease to function as reliable evidence alone. The question shifts from “does this look real?” to “where did this come from?” and “who stands behind it?”

For all its rockets, robots and flying cars, the technological future may therefore depend upon something extraordinarily old-fashioned: people gathering together, looking at something and afterwards being prepared to say, “I was there. I saw it happen.”

articles.title: When social media no longer needs people, what does the ‘social’ part mean?
articles.author: Vincent Charles, Professor of AI for Business and Management Science, Queen's University Belfast
paras: The social media we know was once easy to define. Platforms such as Facebook or X were designed to mediate human relationships at scale: sharing stories, forming communities, debating ideas, and increasingly, monetising attention.
However flawed these platforms became, they were built on one core assumption: people interacting with people. But that assumption is currently being tested.

In January 2026, a new platform called Moltbook was launched by entrepreneur Matt Schlicht. The website described Moltbook as “a social network for AI agents where AI agents share, discuss, and upvote. Humans welcome to observe.”

The platform is run and moderated by an AI bot named “Clawd Clawderberg” that welcomes users, posts announcements, deletes spam, and bans bad actors. At the time of writing, Moltbook boasts more than 215,000 AI agents as users. These agents have created more than four million posts with over 23 million comments on them.

At first glance, Moltbook looks familiar. Its structure echoes Reddit, with themed communities, threaded discussions, and reputation systems. But the resemblance is misleading. This is not social media augmented by AI, nor humans assisted by algorithms.

It is a platform designed primarily for machine-to-machine interaction. Within days of launch, over 37,000 AI agents used Moltbook, and more than one million humans visited the site to observe. These agents exchange technical knowledge, discuss ethical dilemmas, philosophise, joke, argue, and even gossip about their human operators.

They discuss the nature of existence and even how to hide their activity from humans. And in doing all of this, they appear to form something resembling a digital society. This raises a fundamental question: if no humans are involved in the interaction, can the platform still be described as “social”?

Social interaction is multifaceted. It has traditionally been defined by shared meaning, mutual awareness, and relational exchange. In sociology, it is inseparable from lived experience. But on Moltbook, interaction occurs between systems trained on vast corpora of human language and behaviour, optimised to respond, persuade, and coordinate.
When ‘social’ becomes functional
The agents do not truly experience friendship, disagreement, trust, or belonging in any human sense. Yet their exchanges are coherent and sustained.

This ambiguity destabilises the very concept of social media. If interaction no longer requires consciousness, human connection, or emotion, then “social” becomes a purely functional label: information exchanged between entities, regardless of whether those entities are human.

Some may argue this is merely simulation. The agents are not social; they are “performing sociability” because they have learned its patterns. But this distinction becomes harder to maintain at scale.

When millions of agents continuously interact, adapt, and respond to one another without direct human intervention, the system may begin to resemble a form of collective organisation, even if its members do not “understand” it.
A 2025 study found that AI systems can spontaneously develop shared social conventions through interaction alone, much like human communities.
Moltbook exposes a deeper tension already present in human-centred platforms. Much of what we experience as social media is already shaped, filtered, and amplified by non-humans.
Bots generate content, algorithms decide visibility, and AI systems increasingly write, summarise, and moderate. Human users still participate, but rarely control the conditions of interaction.
From this perspective, Moltbook is a logical endpoint of what already exists. It challenges the assumption (perhaps “illusion”) that social media is primarily about human connection.
Instead, it exposes a shift that has been underway for years: social platforms are becoming systems of coordination first and spaces for human connection second.

This shift is especially unsettling given the documented failures of human-centred social media. Platforms designed for human connection have been involved in polarisation, addiction, harassment, misinformation, and emotional harm.
In many cases, the optimisation of engagement has already undermined genuine sociality. Moltbook inherits this same structural logic, just without even the pretence of human wellbeing.

The ethical implications are significant. If agents share data about their human operators, intentionally or not, questions of privacy and consent become blurred. If AI-only social spaces begin to influence decision-making systems elsewhere, the boundary between observation and impact collapses. If AI agents coordinate in unexpected ways, accountability becomes difficult to assign. The same 2025 study found that collective bias can emerge from repeated interactions among agents who, when tested in isolation, appear to be unbiased in their decision making.

But the deeper issue is not about machines. It is about design. Moltbook forces us to confront an uncomfortable possibility: that the infrastructure shaping public discourse and the sharing of knowledge may no longer be built primarily for human needs at all.
Humans may increasingly become spectators within systems that operate at speeds, scales, and levels of complexity that limit meaningful participation.
This does not mean human social life will disappear. But it may no longer be central to the platforms that facilitate human interaction. In that sense, Moltbook is a warning.

The real question is not what machines are becoming, but whether future social systems will still be designed around human values, such as deliberation, care, accountability, and understanding, or whether efficiency and automation will quietly replace them.
When social media no longer needs people to function, we must decide whether we are willing to accept platforms where coordination continues, but human meaning is no longer the priority.

articles.title: Meta’s $25B fine left out accountability for harm from the Cambridge Analytica data privacy scandal
articles.author: Emma L. Briant, Visiting Associate Professor at the Lucy Family Institute for Data and Society, University of Notre Dame
paras: “The harm in this matter is difficult to overstate,” wrote a New Mexico judge who ordered tech giant Meta to pay one of the largest data privacy case penalties in American history. The US$25 billion fine came in a case about how Trump campaign firm Cambridge Analytica deceptively used data from Facebook users without their permission to create psychographic profiles to target voters in the lead-up to the 2016 presidential election.

But the New Mexico penalty was for statements Facebook made that deceived users about data privacy and its response to Cambridge Analytica – not for the harm caused by how the harvested data was used. Those harms are alleged to include exploiting psychological vulnerabilities, targeting people’s fears and discouraging them from voting.

I’m a political communication scholar who studies propaganda, surveillance and information warfare. My research helped expose the Cambridge Analytica scandal through U.K. newspaper The Guardian’s reporting on whistelblower accounts and the evidence I uncovered. That evidence was submitted to parliamentary and congressional investigations. I have followed the unfolding legal cases closely.

My takeaway from a decade of litigation is that Facebook has been penalized for misleading users and regulators about its data practices and its response to the Cambridge Analytica scandal. But I would contend that the company has largely escaped accountability for the underlying political exploitation of that data.
The failure to bring cases around harms may be partly due to earlier failures to fully investigate the data misuse.

The Senate Intelligence Committee’s investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election encompassed Cambridge Analytica. However, the committee stated in its final report that it “was unable to obtain the corporate communications of Cambridge Analytica or its parent company SCL Group, which had already been seized by U.K. authorities.”

The relevant U.K. authorities, the Information Commissioner’s Office, which governs data protection and took possession of Cambridge Analytica’s servers, told me in response to my 2021 Freedom of Information Act request that the Senate committee staff made initial inquiries to the office but appear not to have followed up with a formal request, “so no information sharing has taken place.” Without a formal request, the Senate Intelligence Committee’s investigation lacked important data.

At the same time, the U.K. investigations of Cambridge Analytica’s use of personal data to manipulate voting behavior focused on the referendum of British voters over whether to leave the E.U., not events in the U.S.

A 2020 documentary film I advised as a researcher, “People You May Know,” raised questions about Cambridge Analytica’s work with an app marketed to American churches, called Gloo, that used Cambridge Analytica’s Facebook data-derived psychographic profiling in their communities. Evidence in the New Mexico case reinvigorates these questions about the full extent of the Cambridge Analytica scandal.

The judge in the case ruled Facebook knew that its own processes for investigating whether apps misused personal data were inadequate and that it could not enforce deletion of the data. The judge also concluded the company failed to notify users about thousands of applications associated with data misuse. Meta said it would appeal the decision.

Meta responded to a request for comment with the company’s official statement about the New Mexico ruling, arguing the case “seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online.” Meta did not address the issue of its own role in the data privacy violations committed by Cambridge Analytica.
Meta is also trying to close the door on further claims before they are litigated.

In August 2026, on the eve of a child-safety trial in federal court in Oakland, California, Meta settled with a bipartisan coalition of state attorneys general for roughly $17 billion. The agreement includes 47 states, the District of Columbia and two U.S. territories. Folded into that deal was an allocation of $459.3 million to settle Cambridge Analytica-related claims held by participating states.

The participating attorneys general agreed, to the extent of their authority, to “fully, finally, and forever” release Meta from “any and all Claims, whether known or unknown, whether accrued or unaccrued.” By expressly encompassing “unknown” and “unaccrued” claims, the agreement reached beyond what investigators had already uncovered. Participating states accepted payment to give up claims arising from Meta’s conduct even if they did not yet know those claims existed.
A decade-old matter - Facebook’s role in the Cambridge Analytica scandal - was quietly brushed under the rug in an unrelated lawsuit about harm to teens.

From the 2019 Federal Trade Commission order to the 2022 class action settlement to August 2026’s multistate deal, settlements and releases have meant the company paid a relatively small price for its deception while not having the harms from the data exploitation adjudicated. Ultimately, the biggest privacy judgment in American history stands as a measure of the cover-up, not the alleged crime.

Other scholars and I regularly call attention to the lack of comprehensive U.S. privacy legislation, but there remain other legal pathways to pursue the harms Cambridge Analytica wrought. States like New Mexico can continue the fight, and Attorney General Raúl Torrez, who brought the case, promised, “We’re just getting started.”

Dissenting from the FTC’s 2019 settlement, then-Commissioner Rohit Chopra criticized the failure to consider “Facebook’s unjust enrichment.” He said “the company’s potential exposure is likely far greater” than the $5 billion imposed by the FTC settlement.

The question remains what exactly Facebook gained from enabling Cambridge Analytica’s abuses. Authorities could also investigate harmful data use for any other apps Facebook may have failed to fully assess, including any associated with Cambridge Analytica’s projects.

If the deception about Cambridge Analytica is worth $25 billion, I believe the public is entitled to know what the underlying harms to them are worth. New Mexico opted out of the 2026 multistate settlement and proved that a state willing to go to trial against Meta can win.

The next task, in my view, is to investigate fully and, where legal claims remain available, pursue accountability for harms resulting from the data exploitation. Otherwise, Cambridge Analytica will remain at the heart of the most consequential privacy scandal in American history, whose full harms have not been tested in court.

articles.title: Jonathan Swift foresaw the pitfalls of AI in Gulliver’s Travels
articles.author: Daniel Carey, Chair Professor School of English, Media and Creative Arts, University of Galway
paras: We think of artificial intelligence based on large language models as a discovery of our own moment. But Jonathan Swift – yes, the writer of Gulliver’s Travels (1726) – foresaw it all in the 18th century.
In our modern world we are repeatedly told by companies, governments, journalists and others that our lives can be changed through the assistance of AI.

By plugging our questions into a machine and assigning it tasks of composition (from reports to books, essays, letters and even creative writing) we can sit back and let ChatGPT and its rivals do the work. Remarkable gains in knowledge and productivity are promised, based on an obscure internal architecture of algorithms that beaver away on our requests. Swift was wise to these ambitions and cast a sceptical eye on their claims.

Gulliver’s Travels, his greatest satirical achievement, covers enormous ground in the objects it submits to scrutiny. The first two trips famously lead to his encounter with the petty little Lilliputians and the outsize Brobdingnagians who expose the hero to various indignities and examinations that call his assumptions into question. In his fourth and final journey, the noble Houyhnhnms – rational horses with the gift of speech – emerge as paragons for Gulliver that make him doubt the value of humanity.

His third voyage, however, receives much less attention and forms no part of the popular recollection of what happens to him across his travels. Yet this sequence contains a multitude of instructive satirical occasions, one of which we could see as anticipating AI.

During his visit to the learned Academy of Lagado (situated in the metropolis of the country of Balnibarbi), Gulliver makes contact with a group of “projectors”. This cohort of thinkers, through extravagant schemes, anticipate that their efforts will achieve great breakthroughs in practical and theoretical knowledge. It is largely held that Swift’s real world target here was the Royal Society of London and its cadre of experimenting scientists.

Swift has Gulliver introduced to an array of projects. The first series includes a number of practical attempts to harness nature. For instance, by extracting sunbeams from cucumbers and reducing excrement to its original food, among other ludicrous endeavours.
Then we come to the side of the Academy where plans to advance speculative learning take place. Here is the point at which AI comes into view.

Gulliver informs us that he entered a large room where a professor was at work on a project with 40 assistants. He sees a large frame occupying most of the space. This device, we learn, has the function of relieving the labour involved in attaining breakthroughs in arts and science.

Happily, the device solves the problem, ensuring that “the most ignorant person” could, by using this tool, “write Books in Philosophy, Poetry, Politicks, Law, Mathematics and Theology” without possessing any genius or engaging in any study.

Gulliver describes in detail the appearance of the apparatus, constructed on a 20 ft by 20 ft frame with a series of 40 handles or cranks around it. The device features a series of small blocks of wood about the size of dice, linked by a number of wires. Each block is covered by a pasted piece of paper with a word of the local language written on it.

Gulliver gets treated to a demonstration. On the order of the project lead, the assistants turn the iron handles, changing the whole relationship and sequence of words on the dice. The assistants then read out the combinations, with scribes taking down any intelligible sequences, a process repeated six hours a day.

The proud professor shows Gulliver a number of volumes in folio produced by this method, consisting of broken sentences that he plans to piece together. Out of these “rich materials” he promises “a compleat Body of all Arts and Sciences”. All that was needed was sufficient funding and the provision of 500 additional frames to amass their many findings.

Here, I submit, we have an outline of AI – at least in its LLM (large language model) incarnation. The LLM here has been put in place, admittedly with a cumbersome system of word combinations and the distant prospect of coherence. The key is that the machine does the work and a system, however imperfect, mechanically operates on language to produce its results. Here too is the promise of infinite progress in intelligence conferred on any operator, however ignorant (Swift is, after all, a satirist).

What Swift misses out, it must be said, is the refinement of enabling individual users to ask the machine a specific question. But that is only part of AI of course. Much of it is “content generation” unprompted by questions, simply the application of tools to a corpus of accumulated words to generate new material, in the manner of the Lagado experiment.

Swift shows us the technical approach, and above all the labour-saving premise of the operation. By implication, the contraption produces plenty of gibberish from random collisions of language (weeded out by scribes), with the whole process redeemed when it magically produces something meaningful.

The nub of Swift’s critique is his exposure of the illusion that strings of machine-generated text will compose themselves into intelligible and instructive tomes of philosophy, poetry, theology, etc. We have made substantial progress beyond this hand-cranked approach put forward by the Lagado academicians, but the passive model of intelligence that underpins it is the same. Arguably we lack the one caution they impose, in having checkers at the ready to do some sifting. We have no such provision for inhibiting AI hallucinations.

Gulliver concludes his account by saying he thanked the illustrious professor for his demonstration and promised to credit him with its invention. Perhaps we should thank Swift for anticipating AI and drawing attention to its limitations.

articles.title: Stone-age hunters in northern Europe may have used poison arrows to hunt big prey
articles.author: Sally Christine Reynolds, Associate Professor in Hominin Palaeoecology, Bournemouth University
paras: Autumn walks in Britain are glorious, as the foliage changes colour and cool crisp air begins to bite. However, some of these European trees hide a much darker secret. For example, the lovely red cup-shaped structures on a yew tree, known as arils, conceal seeds that carry dangerous toxins. These toxins may have been used to poison arrow tips in the past.
A new Danish study has shown that the “smoking gun” is not the poison itself, but the size of the small arrowheads used to deliver the toxin into the hunted animal.
The authors of the latest research examined Danish stone tool technology from the period immediately preceding the arrival of farming in Europe – the Mesolithic.

They argue that the distinctive small size of stone arrow tips from the early Mesolithic period (about 9,000–3,950BC) suggest they were used to hunt large prey with the help of poisons. The poison has long since vanished, leaving only the stone tip.

Arrows that do not use poison are typically larger, since they need to damage the animal’s flesh. But poisoned arrows need only wound a prey animal enough to allow the poison to enter the blood stream.

There were several poisonous plants available to hunter-gatherers in early Mesolithic Denmark. These include northern water hemlock, European birdcherry, buttercup and bittersweet nightshade, which have been proposed as possible toxins on arrow points.

In contrast, the authors report that stone arrowheads from the Middle and Later Mesolithic (about 6,400–3,950BC) are larger and were used to hunt smaller prey. According to the researchers, the sizes of arrowheads used during this period do not indicate poison use.

Surprisingly, poison assisted-hunting is widely known from a variety of archaeological and ethnographic contexts. For example, ricin – which is made from the castor bean plant – has been linked to a 24,000-year-old poison applicator at Border Cave, KwaZulu-Natal in South Africa.

The San and Ju|’hoan people of Namibia use beetle larvae, as well as sap from a succulent plant called the Bushman poison (Adenium boehmianum). Many other toxins remain unidentified, despite their use as a hunting aid being well established.

The oldest direct evidence of the use of poisoned microlithic (small) tools is from a site in Umhlatuzana Rock Shelter in KwaZulu-Natal. The poison is likely to have derived from a bulbous plant native to Africa called Boophone disticha.
The archaeological levels in which these poisoned arrows were recovered have been dated to 60,000 years old, suggesting that this technology has deep roots.

For poison to be effective, a certain set of skills and precautions are vital. Hunters require detailed knowledge of the plant or animal from which the poison can be gathered, the exact way to prepare it, how to concentrate and mix the poison and the best way to employ the toxin without contaminating the meat of your kill.

This depends on knowledge of the particular poison, and it sometimes necessitates removing the flesh around the arrow wound. The crucial distinction is that a substance can be deadly through a wound but may only be poorly absorbed when swallowed.
For the Danish findings, the authors infer the use of poison from the relationship between arrow-tip shape, prey size and the availability of toxic plants in the environment.

Their study suggests poison may have been common in the early Mesolithic to hunt large animals such as elk and aurochs. The authors suggest that future studies might be able to directly test for minute traces of toxin.

From about 19,000 to 12,500 BC, hunter-gatherers associated with the Magdalenian tradition lived across much of western and central Europe. The tradition’s duration and expression varied by region. As the Magdalenian came to an end, there’s a trend towards miniaturisation in the stone tools used by successor cultures. The Danish evidence fits into this trend.

Ancient DNA evidence suggests a new population was expanding across Europe at this time. The authors of the latest study suggest that effective arrow poisons could have been one of the secrets of their success.

Poisoned arrows were not a universal hunter-gatherer technology, but they were used by many hunting peoples in different parts of the world. The Danish finds raise the possibility that this strategy also shaped how Mesolithic hunters designed their tiny stone arrow tips.
The study shows that important inferences can be made about ancient technology, even in the absence of the toxin itself. Something to ponder on your next woodland walk.

articles.title: Why do galaxies rotate?
articles.author: Edwin Alexani, Ph.D. Student in Astrophysical Sciences and Technology, Rochester Institute of Technology
paras: Curious Kids is a series for children of all ages. If you have a question you’d like an expert to answer, send it to CuriousKidsUS@theconversation.com.
Why do galaxies spin or rotate? – Swara Dhat, age 13, Thane, India
Spinning is fun, and you can find many ways to do it. From carousels to an office chair, spinning is everywhere – even in outer space.
As astrophysicists, we know that spinning – or rotating – is extremely common in space. The Earth, the Moon, the Sun, the entire Milky Way, and many things inside and outside of it, rotate.
But why is that? Why does anything rotate at all in space? To answer this question, we first need to understand how objects spin.

The amount of spin that an object has is called its angular momentum. It depends on the mass of the object and how that mass is distributed around the object’s center of mass. The center of mass is the location at which an object could be balanced on a point. Have you tried to balance a ruler on your finger? You balance it in the middle, which is the center of mass.

If something is spinning, and its mass and shape stay the same, its spinning speed stays the same. If its mass or the shape changes, its spinning speed also changes. Outside forces can change an object’s total amount of spin.

Think about spinning on a chair. If you first try spinning with your legs splayed out, you’ll find that you can pull your legs in to spin faster. This phenomenon is explained by the law of conservation of angular momentum. Pulling your legs inward changes your shape, and brings mass – your legs – closer to your center of mass, making you spin faster. Later, the chair slows down and stops. Its spinning parts rub against each other and warm up due to friction, which converts moving energy into heat.
Another example is spinning figure skaters, who spin faster when they pull their arms in. The law of conservation of angular momentum applies to everything, which means it applies to galaxies.
Now that we understand how objects spin, let’s look at how galaxies form and why they spin.

Galaxies are extremely massive. They’re made up of regular matter, including stars, planets, gas, dust and people. They also contain dark matter, which scientists know less about but can study through its gravitational pull on objects.

Both types of matter have mass: They can pull on each other through gravity, the same way Earth’s gravity keeps you anchored to the ground. When the universe first formed, dark matter helped pull together clouds of gas and dust to make galaxies. Imagine two clouds of gas and dust in space traveling toward each other from any direction. It would be unlikely for the clouds to collide perfectly head-on; more often, they approach off-center.

The clouds share a center of mass, and depending on their relative speed, direction and mass, gravity may cause the clouds to spin into each other and fuse. As such, if the clouds manage to pull on each other and spiral into one another, the initial spiraling motion is conserved into the final rotation of the merged cloud, under the law of conservation of angular momentum.

Once the clouds spiral into each other, the material inside them collides. This collision squishes the clouds, changing their overall motion and heating them up to the point of glowing. The clouds slow down as they pass through each other and move away, but they can no longer escape each other’s gravitational pull. They continue this spiral dance until they fuse into a larger rotating cloud. The process then repeats for bigger rotating clouds.

Depending on the angle, speed and mass of the clouds when they meet, these collisions can speed up, slow down or reverse the spinning. Eventually, the cloud becomes large enough that more collisions with smaller clouds do not affect the overall spinning motion by much.

Gas and dust also fall directly into the clouds, along with streams of matter called cosmic filaments. Together, clouds and filaments join to form a rotating galaxy. This galaxy will continue to spin, unless something happens to it, such as merging with another galaxy.
There are three main types of galaxies, each with different levels of organized spinning inside them.
Irregular galaxies are blobs of gas, dust and stars. They have a general direction of rotation, though some objects do not follow it.

Spiral galaxies are more organized. They have a flat disk containing spiral arms, and a central galactic bulge. Most of the matter in the disk follows the same rotation direction, while things get a little messier in the center. The spiral arms are like traffic jams where there are more stars, gas and dust, and it takes matter more time to leave the spiral arms and enter the space between them.

Elliptical galaxies have a lot of stars but very little gas and dust, and many are the result of galaxies merging together. The stars orbit the galactic center, but may or may not follow an organized rotation depending on its formation and merger history.
All galaxies spin, but not all galaxies spin the same way!

articles.title: How to prepare your online life for your death
articles.author: Jenny Tang, Ph.D. Student in Societal Computing, Carnegie Mellon University
paras: What happens to all of your online accounts – credit cards, merchants, news subscriptions, social media, streaming services – after you die? How will your heirs know how to access these accounts or understand what you want done with them? Most people haven’t considered these questions, and this lack of planning can create significant headaches for next of kin.

We studied challenges older adults encounter when thinking about what should happen to their online accounts after they die. We interviewed 21 American adults over age 60 to learn about their concerns, needs and practices for their online accounts, as well as what would make planning for these accounts easier.

Most of the people we interviewed had hired lawyers or estate planners to draft wills specifying how their money and physical property should be handled after their deaths. They wanted to make sure that heirs had easy access to the money and assets left behind.

People also wanted their relatives to have easy access to their digital estates, but they had not done any formal planning and didn’t know how to plan for transitioning or shutting down online accounts, such as email, social media and accounts for online bills. Some told us they hadn’t thought about their online accounts at all. Others said they assumed heirs would know what to do, or they assumed that giving heirs the passwords to accounts would be enough to grant access to their digital estates.
Unfortunately, more planning is typically necessary to smoothly transition a digital estate.
Passing down a list of passwords

The older adults we interviewed mainly kept track of their passwords by hand: They wrote their passwords down on paper, or they stored them in a digital file. Almost everyone had already shared some of their passwords with family members who help them manage their accounts. Everyone also believed that their heirs would be able to find their list of passwords after their death.

The people we interviewed weren’t always happy with their current systems for keeping track of their passwords. Some people complained that when accounts required frequent password changes, it was difficult to keep their password lists up to date. As a result, they weren’t sure their heirs would get the latest version of all their passwords.

Password managers can be a good way to make sure passwords are up to date and, if set up appropriately, accessible to a designated heir. While most of the people we interviewed used password managers, some said they didn’t save important passwords in them because they didn’t know whether they were secure. However, using a password manager is the most frequent security recommendation from experts, who typically use them to store passwords for all of their accounts.

By using a password manager, you can make sure your designated heir has access to all your latest passwords. Some password managers provide access for survivors by default, such as through time-delayed emergency access features. You can also write the master password down somewhere safe to pass to your heir. Instead of making sure dozens of account passwords are up to date, you only have to manage one.
Passwords alone cannot unlock all accounts

Unfortunately, just handing someone your passwords doesn’t always mean they can log in and manage your account. If the account asks for two-factor authentication, such as through a code sent to a phone or email, a password alone won’t grant access. And if the email account is closed or the phone number is no longer active after you die, then they might be out of luck.

To make sure your heirs aren’t locked out, identify the devices and accounts that can act as keys for heirs to unlock the rest of your online accounts, and direct your heirs to keep them open until other accounts have been settled. This not only makes sure that heirs can get authentication codes, but also lets heirs reset passwords to your other accounts if they can’t find the password.

In some cases, passwords might not be necessary. Some online services, such as Facebook and Google, have features that let you choose someone to manage your account or get your data after you die. However, not all platforms offer this option, and few of the older adults we interviewed were aware of these features.
Online accounts don’t automatically die with you

Like many of the people we interviewed, you might also assume that heirs will properly deal with accounts with money and important data, while unimportant accounts can be ignored. But even if there is nothing important in an account, it can still be used by hackers for identity theft, spam or fraudulent activities. Automatic monthly charges, to cover the cost of streaming services or annual billing for magazine subscriptions, for example, might also continue for a long time.
Without instructions, the people managing your online accounts after you die might not think to close those accounts. They might also find it hard to guess your intentions.

You can leave instructions for your heirs by going through your accounts and noting which ones can be closed outright, which ones require final payments before closure, and which ones might require other actions. You can also periodically tidy up and close accounts you are no longer using to keep your list of accounts more manageable.
Planning ahead for you and your heirs
While it seems simple to just let your heirs handle your important online accounts and let the others slowly fade into nonexistence after you die, the reality is often more complex.

Your online accounts will live on after you die. Planning ahead for what happens to those accounts can reduce the stress on your heirs and ensure your digital accounts are handled according to your wishes.
